subject: Copywriting
title: Reciprocity: Give First, Sell Later
description: Learn Reciprocity: Give First, Sell Later in one minute.

hook.text: Hare Krishna members gave flowers at airports. Recipients felt obligated and donated. The gift created a debt.

buildup.text: Cialdini's reciprocity principle: when someone gives you something, you feel compelled to give back.

discovery.text: Free trials, free ebooks, free samples—all reciprocity in action. The 'free' thing creates a psychological IOU.

twist.text: Reciprocity works even when the gift is unwanted. You feel obligated even if you toss the flower in the trash.

climax.text: The best marketing gives genuine value first. Reciprocity only works long-term when the gift is real.

punchline.text: Give value first. The sale follows naturally.

quiz.question: What is the reciprocity principle in copywriting?
options: Giving something to create an obligation to return the favor

details.summary: Reciprocity is the deep human instinct to return favors. When brands give something valuable first — a free guide, a helpful tool, genuine advice — they create a psychological obligation that makes prospects more receptive to eventual sales pitches.
details.whyItMatters: Reciprocity is the foundation of content marketing, lead magnets, and free trials. Understanding why giving first works helps copywriters design customer journeys that build genuine goodwill before asking for money.
takeaways: Free value creates psychological obligation in the receiver
The gift must feel genuinely helpful, not like a thinly disguised sales pitch
Reciprocity works best when the initial gift is unexpected

faq.question: Why does giving something free lead to sales?
faq.answer: Humans have a deep-seated need to return favors — it's wired into our social nature. When a brand provides genuine value for free, recipients feel an unconscious debt. They're more likely to buy, engage, or share because doing so resolves the feeling of owing something.

faq.question: What makes a good lead magnet?
faq.answer: A good lead magnet solves a specific, immediate problem for the target audience. It should deliver real value — not just tease it — so the recipient thinks 'if the free stuff is this good, the paid product must be amazing.' Checklists, templates, and mini-courses work well.
